Package io.thymekit

Interface Composable<K>

All Known Implementing Classes:
Breadcrumbs.Builder, Caption.Builder, Element, Element.Descriptor, Heading.Builder, Hero.Builder, Md.Builder, Section.Builder, Topbar.Builder
Functional Interface:
This is a functional interface and can therefore be used as the assignment target for a lambda expression or method reference.
@FunctionalInterface public interface Composable<K>
Something that becomes an element. Every builder in the kit implements it, and so does Element itself — an element is what has already become one, so build() hands back the same value.

That is why a place that takes an element takes this instead: with the currency implementing it, the signature says "whatever becomes an element" and covers both without an "or" in it. A page reads the way the concept does, with nothing between one element and the next: 


 PageModel.of(model)
     .title(it.name())
     .add(Hero.of(Heading.h1(it.name()))
         .eyebrow(Caption.eyebrow("Catalogue"))
         .subtitle(Caption.subtitle(it.latinName())))
     .render("ingredient-page");

build() keeps one meaning of its own: settle it, because you want to hold it — in a variable, in a list, in a field. What is settled is a value and cannot change afterwards.

The kit accepts a Composable and never stores one: every place that takes one builds it at once, so a half-made element never lives anywhere. Writing an element of your own does not require implementing this — a factory that returns an Element is an element factory, because an element is recognised by what it is, not by what it implements.

It has one method, so a lambda is one too, and that is deliberate: a type of yours that already knows how to describe itself becomes composable with () -> myThing.asElement() and goes into a page beside the kit's own. Since everything is settled where it is taken, nothing is deferred by writing it that way.
